entities.name: Attila the Hun
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Attila (c. 406–453 CE), known as the 'Scourge of God' (Flagellum Dei), was the ruler of the Hunnic Empire who terrorized both the Eastern and Western Roman Empires — the most feared conqueror of Late Antiquity and the embodiment of nomadic barbarian power.

Ruling a vast steppe empire from the Ural Mountains to the Rhine, he extorted enormous tributes from Constantinople and invaded the Western Empire in 451 CE. His massive army — a polyglot horde of Huns, Goths, and Gepids — was stopped at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains by a coalition led by the Roman general Aetius and Visigothic king Theodoric I.

He invaded Italy in 452, sacking cities from Aquileia to Milan. Legend holds that Pope Leo I personally persuaded Attila to withdraw from Rome — one of the most famous encounters between spiritual and temporal power.

He died suddenly on his wedding night (453 CE), reportedly of a nosebleed. His empire collapsed within a year. The refugees fleeing his Italian invasion are traditionally credited with founding Venice's lagoon settlements.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Attila's invasion of Italy in 452 CE led to Pope Leo I's direct intervention, which resulted in Attila's withdrawal from Rome. This event highlights the significant impact of Attila on European politics and the power dynamics between the Eastern Roman Empire and the barbarian kingdoms.
